Equine anesthesia · Oxygen transport

Equine Anesthesia: Oxygenation and Tissue Oxygen Delivery

Oxygenation, circulation and tissue oxygen delivery in equine anesthesia, drawing on Hubbell and Muir and the equine experimental record.

By Archil Jaliashvili · BHOC Veterinary · 31 Oct 2026

Oxygen delivery during equine anesthesiaThe Hubbell and Muir frameworkRead blood measurements with circulationCardiac output and gas exchange: the equine experimentThe pharmacokinetic record in horsesThe equine development priorities for BHOC

Oxygen delivery during equine anesthesia

Equine anesthesia requires attention to pulmonary oxygenation, oxygen-carrying capacity and circulation. These are connected physiological functions with distinct measurements. Their interpretation determines how an equine oxygen-delivery study is designed. [1, 2]

Hubbell and Muir examined oxygenation, oxygen delivery and methods of improving each in their Equine Veterinary Journal review. The article appeared online in 2014 and in the January 2015 issue. It is part of the BHOC scientific catalogue. [1]

The Hubbell and Muir framework

The review brings pulmonary oxygenation and peripheral oxygen delivery into the same assessment. It examines the published approaches to improving each and records their variable results and clinical applicability. [1]

For equine research, this provides a practical starting point: identify the physiological limitation, select the relevant measurement and evaluate the outcome. A change in arterial oxygenation and a change in oxygen delivery answer different questions. [1, 2]

Read blood measurements with circulation

Packed cell volume describes red-cell volume. Hemoglobin contributes oxygen-carrying capacity. Blood flow, oxygen affinity, unloading and tissue demand determine how that capacity translates into functional oxygen delivery. [2]

An equine study needs a measurement plan that connects these functions. Record the blood compartment, the circulatory measurement and the clinical outcome. This gives each result a physiological meaning. [2]

Cardiac output and gas exchange: the equine experiment

Swanson and Muir studied dobutamine in healthy horses anesthetized with halothane in lateral or dorsal recumbency. Higher tested infusion rates increased cardiac output. The reported gas-exchange measures did not significantly improve. [3]

Dorsal recumbency produced a larger alveolar-to-arterial oxygen difference and shunt fraction than lateral positioning. The study demonstrates the distinction between a circulatory response and a pulmonary gas-exchange response in that anesthetic model. [3]

The pharmacokinetic record in horses

Soma and colleagues studied hemoglobin glutamer-200 bovine in horses in 2005. Median elimination half-lives were 1.3 hours for smaller polymer aggregates and 12.0 hours for larger aggregates. Polymer size was associated with different elimination profiles in the tested preparation. [4]

This establishes a specific equine pharmacokinetic record for that carrier. It also makes molecular composition an essential part of interpreting exposure and planning further equine studies. [4]

The equine development priorities for BHOC

BHOC, Biological Hemoglobin Oxygen Carrier, focuses on tissue oxygen support within Precision Oxygen Therapeutics. Equine development requires a characterized formulation, a specified anesthetic setting, an appropriate comparison and species-specific monitoring. [5]

The study plan should connect oxygen-related measurements with a clinical endpoint, including recovery where relevant. The population, timing of observations and outcome measures need to be specified before the study begins.

The equine transfusion guide addresses donor access and compatibility. This article addresses anesthesia and functional oxygen delivery. Together, they connect the available blood supply with the physiological task of delivering oxygen to tissues.

BHOC Veterinary Therapeutics, also known as BHOC Vet, is led by Archil Jaliashvili. The BHOC Species & Biodiversity Protection Initiative connects oxygen delivery science with the future of animal health and species protection.

Our foundation is comparative biology: different species have different blood group systems, yet most vertebrates share hemoglobin-based oxygen transport. We explore how this foundation can inform species-specific research and development.
